title: Genetic Diversity in Populations

lessons.title: Populations, gene pools and genetic variation
lessons.question: What changes when a population evolves?
lessons.goal: Define a gene pool and distinguish change in a population from change within an individual.
lessons.prior: Individuals carry alleles. Inheritance passes alleles between generations, while population size can also change.

terms.meaning: Individuals of the same species occupying a defined area during a defined time.
terms.example: The breeding rabbits in a specified valley during one season form the study population.
terms.importantDistinction: A population boundary must be stated before counting frequencies.
terms.misconception: A population is every organism of every species in an ecosystem.

terms.meaning: All the alleles present in the reproductive population being considered.
terms.example: A population contains several alleles at many different loci.
terms.importantDistinction: A gene pool describes a population, not only one individual’s genotype.
terms.misconception: A gene pool is the set of organs inside one organism.

terms.meaning: Differences in genetic information among individuals or lineages.
terms.example: Individuals carry different alleles at a pigment locus.
terms.importantDistinction: Not all phenotypic variation is genetic.
terms.misconception: Every visible difference must be caused by a different allele.

terms.meaning: A change in allele frequencies in a population across generations.
terms.example: An allele’s proportion changes from 0.30 to 0.45 between sampled generations.
terms.importantDistinction: A larger population can retain the same allele frequencies.
terms.misconception: Any increase in population size is automatically an allele-frequency change.

sections: Define the population you are studying

Population genetics studies the genetic composition of populations and how that composition changes. A population consists of individuals of the same species within a defined place and time. Those boundaries matter: counting one breeding colony is not the same as counting every colony across a continent.

The gene pool is the collection of alleles present in that population. An individual carries only part of the population’s variation. At an ordinary diploid autosomal locus, each individual contributes two allele copies.
Track proportions across generations

Microevolution is a change in allele frequencies across generations. An allele frequency is its share of all allele copies at the locus. It is a proportion, not simply the number of individuals showing a trait.

Suppose a population doubles in size while every allele’s proportion stays the same. The number of copies increases, but the allele frequencies have not changed. Conversely, frequencies can change even if the total population size remains constant.
An individual’s body can grow, develop or adjust to conditions. Those changes are not themselves evidence that a population’s inherited allele frequencies have changed.
Distinguish genetic and environmental differences

Genetic variation can influence phenotypes, but environment and gene regulation also matter. A plant grown in shade may differ from a genetically similar plant grown in bright light. That observation alone does not identify an allele-frequency change.

To study evolution at a locus, specify the alleles and measure or infer their frequencies with appropriate evidence. Later lessons explain when genotype counts permit direct counting and when a mathematical model is required.
Do not assume every genetic difference is advantageous, or that evolution always moves toward greater size or complexity. The mechanisms can include selection and chance.

worked.title: Count change versus frequency change
worked.scenario: A population grows from 100 to 200 diploid individuals. Allele A rises from 60 of 200 copies to 120 of 400 copies.
steps: At the first sampling, A frequency is 60/200 = 0.30.
At the second, it is 120/400 = 0.30.
The number of A copies doubled but its proportion did not.
These measurements show no allele-frequency change at this locus over the interval.

lessons.title: Allele frequencies and genotype frequencies
lessons.question: Why do allele calculations usually use twice as many copies as individuals?
lessons.goal: Calculate genotype and allele frequencies directly from diploid genotype counts.
lessons.prior: At a diploid autosomal locus, an individual carries two allele copies, even when both are the same.

terms.meaning: The proportion of individuals with a specified genotype.
terms.example: Thirty AA individuals in a population of 100 give frequency 0.30.
terms.importantDistinction: Its denominator is the number of individuals sampled.
terms.misconception: Genotype frequency always divides by twice the population size.

terms.meaning: The proportion of allele copies represented by a particular allele at a locus.
terms.example: Twenty A copies among 50 copies give frequency 0.40.
terms.importantDistinction: For an ordinary diploid autosomal sample, the denominator is 2N.
terms.misconception: An AA individual contributes only one A copy.

terms.meaning: The contribution of one copy of each allele from a heterozygous individual.
terms.example: Each Aa individual contributes one A and one a to the allele count.
terms.importantDistinction: Count both copies, not half an individual.
terms.misconception: A heterozygote contributes two dominant alleles.

terms.meaning: The requirement that mutually exclusive complete categories account for the whole sample.
terms.example: At a two-allele locus, p + q = 1.
terms.importantDistinction: The relevant categories and denominator must be consistent.
terms.misconception: Genotype frequencies and allele frequencies may be mixed in one sum without distinction.

sections: Count individuals for genotype frequencies
Let N be the number of diploid individuals sampled at a two-allele autosomal locus. The possible genotypes are AA, Aa and aa. Genotype frequency is the number with one genotype divided by N.
For 30 AA, 50 Aa and 20 aa individuals, N = 100. The frequencies are 0.30, 0.50 and 0.20. They add to 1 because every sampled individual belongs to exactly one of these genotype categories.
Count copies for allele frequencies
The same sample contains 2N = 200 allele copies. Each AA contributes two A copies, each Aa contributes one A and one a, and each aa contributes two a copies.
The A count is 2(30) + 50 = 110, so p = 110/200 = 0.55. The a count is 2(20) + 50 = 90, so q = 90/200 = 0.45. The allele frequencies also add to 1.

The general relationships are p = [2(AA) + Aa]/2N and q = [2(aa) + Aa]/2N, where the genotype symbols inside the brackets represent counts. Write units or category names beside the numbers so that individuals are not mistaken for allele copies.
Direct counting does not need equilibrium
When all genotype counts are known, allele frequencies can be calculated directly. You do not need to assume Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium to count copies.

A recessive phenotype alone provides different information. Under a simple complete-dominance model, it identifies aa individuals but does not separate AA from Aa among dominant-phenotype individuals. Additional assumptions would be needed to infer all allele frequencies from that phenotype count alone.
Check every calculation: genotype counts total N, allele counts total 2N, and both sets of frequencies separately sum to 1.

lessons.title: The Hardy–Weinberg model and its assumptions
lessons.question: What does a non-evolving reference model allow us to predict?
lessons.goal: Explain the model’s conditions and distinguish allele totals from expected genotype frequencies.
lessons.prior: For two alleles, p + q = 1 by definition. Direct allele counts are possible when genotypes are known.

terms.meaning: A model in which allele frequencies remain constant and genotype frequencies follow p², 2pq and q² under stated conditions.
terms.example: A large randomly mating population with no selection, migration or mutation is the reference model.
terms.importantDistinction: The model is a baseline to test, not an automatic property of every population.
terms.misconception: Any population with a recessive phenotype must be in equilibrium.

terms.meaning: Mating that is independent of the genotype being considered.
terms.example: Gamete combinations can be modelled from allele frequencies without genotype-based mate preference.
terms.importantDistinction: Random mating at one locus does not mean every behaviour is random.
terms.misconception: Random mating means every pair produces an identical number and genotype of offspring.

terms.meaning: The expected frequency of one homozygous genotype under a two-allele Hardy–Weinberg model.
terms.example: If p = 0.70, the expected AA frequency is 0.49.
terms.importantDistinction: It is an expected genotype frequency, not another allele frequency.
terms.misconception: p² is always the frequency of the A allele itself.

terms.meaning: The expected heterozygote frequency under the two-allele Hardy–Weinberg model.
terms.example: Aa can form from A then a or a then A.
terms.importantDistinction: The factor two counts the two ways to form a heterozygote.
terms.misconception: The heterozygote frequency is pq because only one parental direction is possible.

sections: Start with the allele pool
At a locus with two alleles, let p be the frequency of A and q the frequency of a. Because these are the complete allele categories, p + q = 1. This identity does not require equilibrium.

If gametes combine randomly with those frequencies, AA has expected frequency p × p = p² and aa has q × q = q². A heterozygote can arise as A from one gamete and a from the other, or the reverse. Its total expected frequency is pq + qp = 2pq.
Name the conditions rather than hiding them

The Hardy–Weinberg reference model assumes a very large population, random mating with respect to the locus, no mutation, no migration and no natural selection affecting the alleles or genotypes. A very large population minimizes chance fluctuations from sampling.

Under these idealized conditions, allele frequencies remain constant across generations and genotype proportions follow p² + 2pq + q² = 1. The model gives a baseline for asking whether observed data fit the prediction.
A real population need not satisfy every condition perfectly. A mismatch can suggest that assumptions need investigation, but the mismatch alone does not identify which mechanism caused it.
Dominance is not the cause of frequency

The letters p and q can represent the two alleles whether or not one is dominant. In familiar complete-dominance problems, p often names the dominant allele and q the recessive allele. This notation does not make p larger than q.
Dominance determines the heterozygote’s phenotype. It does not determine the allele’s frequency or guarantee that the dominant allele is favoured by selection.

When only the recessive phenotype count is given, identifying q² and taking its square root requires the stated equilibrium and phenotype-model assumptions. Without them, do not silently infer the unobserved genotypes.

worked.title: Derive a heterozygote prediction
worked.scenario: At a two-allele locus, p = 0.70 and q = 0.30. Assume Hardy–Weinberg conditions.
steps: AA expectation is 0.70 × 0.70 = 0.49.
aa expectation is 0.30 × 0.30 = 0.09.
Aa expectation is 2 × 0.70 × 0.30 = 0.42.
These genotype predictions depend on the model, unlike the allele total p + q = 1.

lessons.title: Calculating expected genotype frequencies
lessons.question: How do you move from a recessive phenotype count to expected carrier numbers?
lessons.goal: Solve Hardy–Weinberg problems with explicit assumptions, separate quantities and reasonableness checks.
lessons.prior: Under the stated model, recessive phenotype aa has frequency q², not q.

terms.meaning: The expected aa genotype frequency under a two-allele Hardy–Weinberg model.
terms.example: If q is 0.40, q² is 0.16.
terms.importantDistinction: A recessive phenotype fraction can be used as q² only with the appropriate model.
terms.misconception: The recessive phenotype fraction always equals q directly.

terms.meaning: The proportion of heterozygotes carrying a recessive allele in the stated model.
terms.example: For Hardy–Weinberg p = 0.60 and q = 0.40, carriers have frequency 0.48.
terms.importantDistinction: For this simple recessive model, carriers are heterozygotes, not all individuals with a.
terms.misconception: Every carrier is homozygous recessive.

terms.meaning: A model-predicted number obtained by multiplying a frequency by population size.
terms.example: A frequency of 0.48 in N = 200 gives 96 expected individuals.
terms.importantDistinction: Expected counts need not be exactly realized in a finite sample.
terms.misconception: An expected count guarantees the exact outcome in every sample.

terms.meaning: Recovering q from q² when the Hardy–Weinberg assumptions apply.
terms.importantDistinction: Taking a square root is not the same as dividing the frequency by two.
terms.misconception: If q² is 0.16, q must be 0.08.

sections: Identify the given quantity

Suppose a recessive phenotype occurs in 32 of 200 individuals and the problem explicitly assumes Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium with complete dominance. The observed aa fraction is 32/200 = 0.16, which is used as q².
Take the square root to obtain the recessive allele frequency: q = √0.16 = 0.40. Then p = 1 − q = 0.60. Do not call 0.16 the allele frequency; it describes individuals with two recessive copies.
Predict genotypes and convert to counts
Use the allele frequencies to calculate the expected genotype frequencies: p² = 0.36, 2pq = 0.48 and q² = 0.16. These are the expected fractions of AA, Aa and aa individuals.
To obtain counts, multiply each frequency by N = 200. The expected numbers are 72 AA, 96 Aa and 32 aa. Check that the counts total 200 and the frequencies total 1.
The heterozygotes are carriers in this simple recessive model. The dominant-phenotype fraction includes AA and Aa together, so it is 0.36 + 0.48 = 0.84, not p alone.
Keep precision until the final answer

Carry sufficient decimal precision through square roots and multiplication. Round the final expected number to an appropriate whole individual only after completing the calculation. Rounding q too early can noticeably change a carrier estimate.
If allele frequency is already given, start with that value instead of taking another square root. If all genotype counts are given, direct allele counting may be the appropriate first method.

A strong answer states the model, labels each quantity, shows the calculation and interprets the result. A bare number makes it difficult to see whether the correct denominator and assumption were used.

worked.title: Estimate carriers for a rare recessive condition
worked.scenario: In a hypothetical population at Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, 1 in 10 000 individuals has a fully recessive phenotype.
steps: Carrier frequency = 2pq = 2(0.99)(0.01) = 0.0198.
As a percentage, this is 1.98%, not 0.0198%.
The inference depends on the stated model; it is not a personal medical-risk estimate.

lessons.title: Using population data to test a prediction
lessons.question: How can the same allele frequencies produce different genotype patterns?
lessons.goal: Compare observed and expected genotype counts without claiming that one mismatch identifies its cause.
lessons.prior: Direct counts yield observed allele frequencies. The Hardy–Weinberg model predicts genotype proportions from those frequencies.

terms.meaning: A count actually supplied or measured in the sample.
terms.example: A sample contains 40 AA, 20 Aa and 40 aa individuals.
terms.importantDistinction: Observed and expected values must be kept separate.
terms.misconception: An observed count is whatever the formula predicts.

terms.meaning: The genotype proportions predicted by the selected model.
terms.example: For p = q = 0.50, Hardy–Weinberg predicts 0.25 AA, 0.50 Aa and 0.25 aa.
terms.importantDistinction: A prediction can be compared with observations rather than substituted for them.
terms.misconception: Expected proportions must equal every observed sample exactly.

terms.meaning: Differences that arise because a finite sample does not reproduce population proportions perfectly.
terms.example: Two small samples can show different counts by chance.
terms.importantDistinction: A small mismatch is not automatically strong evidence of a specific mechanism.
terms.misconception: Every difference between samples proves natural selection.

terms.meaning: Evaluation of how well observations fit a model’s predictions.
terms.example: Observed heterozygotes are compared with the expected 2pq fraction.
terms.importantDistinction: Agreement does not prove every assumption; mismatch does not identify one cause alone.
terms.misconception: A mismatch uniquely identifies mutation as the cause.

sections: Calculate the observed allele pool first
Suppose a sample has 40 AA, 20 Aa and 40 aa individuals. There are 100 individuals and 200 allele copies. A copies total 80 + 20 = 100, so p = 0.50; q is also 0.50.

These allele frequencies are directly observed from genotype counts. Under Hardy–Weinberg, they predict 25 AA, 50 Aa and 25 aa individuals in a sample of 100. The observed sample contains fewer heterozygotes than that prediction.
A genotype mismatch is not a unique explanation

A shortage of heterozygotes could be associated with non-random mating, population structure or other processes. The counts alone do not uniquely establish which mechanism acted. Sampling and measurement also need consideration.

Notice that the observed sample and the predicted distribution have the same p and q. Genotype proportions can differ while allele frequencies remain the same. Non-random mating can alter genotype proportions without necessarily changing allele frequencies by itself.
Keep two questions separate: do genotype proportions fit the random-mating model, and have allele frequencies changed across generations? They require related but different comparisons.
Use consistent sampling and restrained conclusions

To compare generations, sample the same defined population and locus using comparable methods. A change in p or q supports allele-frequency change at that locus, but a different sampling location or age group can complicate interpretation.

Agreement with a prediction is not proof that every Hardy–Weinberg condition is perfectly satisfied. Opposing effects can sometimes balance, and finite samples have limited resolution. A visible mismatch is a reason to investigate, not permission to name a mechanism without evidence.
These activities use direct comparisons and arithmetic. Formal statistical testing may be useful in research, but no unsupported significance claim is needed here.

lessons.title: Natural selection and non-random mating
lessons.question: How do survival and mating success affect inherited variation?
lessons.goal: Explain selection through differential reproductive success and distinguish it from mate-pairing effects.
lessons.prior: Allele frequency describes copies in a population. A phenotype can affect survival or reproduction in a particular environment.

terms.meaning: Differential reproductive success associated with heritable variation in a particular environment.
terms.example: A heritable resistance trait improves survival and subsequent reproduction under a specific challenge.
terms.importantDistinction: The environment influences which variants contribute more descendants.
terms.misconception: Selection gives organisms the exact new mutation they need.

terms.meaning: Reproductive contribution compared with other genotypes or phenotypes in the relevant setting.
terms.example: One genotype leaves more surviving reproductive descendants under the stated conditions.
terms.importantDistinction: Fitness is not simply physical strength or long life.
terms.misconception: The largest individual must always have the highest fitness.

terms.meaning: Selection associated with differences in mating success.
terms.example: A heritable courtship trait affects the probability of obtaining mates.
terms.importantDistinction: A mating advantage can occur even when a trait has survival costs.
terms.misconception: A sexually selected trait must always improve survival in every environment.

terms.meaning: Mating patterns that depend on characteristics related to the genotype being studied.
terms.example: Individuals preferentially mate with others having a similar phenotype.
terms.importantDistinction: It can alter genotype proportions without automatically changing allele frequencies by itself.
terms.misconception: Non-random pairing must always change p and q immediately.

sections: Follow reproduction, not intention

Individuals vary, and some variation is heritable. If a heritable trait affects survival or reproduction, the associated alleles may be represented differently in the next generation. Natural selection describes that differential reproductive contribution.

The environment matters. A trait advantageous in one setting may have little benefit or a cost elsewhere. Fitness therefore refers to contribution to future generations in context, not simply strength, speed or size.
Selection does not make an organism deliberately produce a needed mutation. Variation must exist or arise independently before its consequences can affect reproductive success.
Distinguish survival from mating success
A trait can increase survival but reduce mating opportunities, or increase mating success while imposing a survival cost. Sexual selection focuses on differences in obtaining mates and reproducing.

For example, a conspicuous display might attract mates while also increasing exposure to predators. The overall evolutionary effect depends on the balance of reproductive consequences, not on whether the display appears efficient to an observer.
A claim that selection occurred needs evidence relating heritable differences to reproductive outcomes. A change in frequency alone can also arise through chance or movement between populations.
Pairing patterns and allele totals are different

Non-random mating changes who pairs with whom. It can change genotype frequencies, such as increasing homozygosity, without directly changing allele frequencies if all alleles retain the same overall reproductive contribution.

Sexual selection and non-random mating are related but not identical statements. When mating success differs, some individuals contribute more offspring. When only pairing patterns differ, allele totals need not immediately change.
Use the information in the case to identify what varies: pairing, survival, number of offspring, or several together.

lessons.title: Genetic drift, bottlenecks and founder effects
lessons.question: How can an allele become common without providing an advantage?
lessons.goal: Distinguish chance sampling from selection and compare bottleneck and founder cases.
lessons.prior: Finite populations pass on only a sample of existing allele copies in each generation.

terms.meaning: Random change in allele frequencies caused by chance sampling in finite populations.
terms.example: By chance, carriers of one allele leave fewer descendants in a small population.
terms.importantDistinction: Drift does not require the allele to affect survival or mating success.
terms.misconception: Every frequency increase proves the allele is beneficial.

terms.meaning: A change in genetic composition associated with a sharp reduction in population size.
terms.example: A small surviving subset carries only part of the earlier variation.
terms.importantDistinction: A demographic recovery does not automatically restore lost alleles.
terms.misconception: Returning to the original population size automatically restores every lost allele.

terms.meaning: A change in allele representation when a small subset establishes a new population.
terms.example: A few colonists carry frequencies different from the source population by chance.
terms.importantDistinction: The original large population need not be destroyed.
terms.misconception: Founder effects require the original population to go extinct.

terms.meaning: An allele reaching frequency 1 at the locus in the population considered.
terms.example: Only A remains among sampled reproductive copies.
terms.importantDistinction: Fixation describes the locus and population, not the absence of variation everywhere.
terms.misconception: Fixation of one allele means every gene in the species is identical.

sections: Chance can change the sample

Not every individual leaves the same number of descendants. In a finite population, chance differences can change allele frequencies even when the alleles have no effect on survival or reproduction. This is genetic drift.

Drift has a stronger relative effect in small populations because a small number of births, deaths or reproductive events can represent a large fraction of the gene pool. An allele may be lost or become fixed by chance.

A useful distinction is whether the case links reproductive success with a heritable trait. Trait-related differences support selection; random sampling independent of the trait supports drift. Both processes can operate together.
A bottleneck samples the original population

A bottleneck occurs when population size falls sharply. The survivors may carry a smaller and unrepresentative sample of the earlier alleles. If the reduction is random with respect to a studied allele, drift can strongly change that allele’s frequency.

If the population later increases, descendants reproduce the variation that survived. Recovery in numbers does not automatically bring back alleles that were lost. Mutation or gene flow might introduce variation later, but population growth alone does not guarantee restoration.
Founders establish a new gene pool
A founder effect occurs when a small group starts a new population. The founders may carry allele frequencies different from those of the source population simply because they are a small sample.
The source population can remain large and intact. That separates the founder case from a bottleneck that reduces an existing population. Both involve sampling, but the demographic history differs.
Do not infer that a newly common allele must be adaptive. A small island population can have unusual allele frequencies because of its founders even before evidence of local selection is available.

lessons.title: Gene flow and mutation
lessons.question: How do alleles enter a population or arise for the first time?
lessons.goal: Distinguish movement of existing alleles from the creation of new sequence variants.
lessons.prior: A founder event samples a source population. Continued movement and new mutations can also alter genetic composition.

terms.meaning: Transfer of alleles between populations through successful genetic contribution.
terms.example: Migrants reproduce in another population, introducing allele copies.
terms.importantDistinction: Movement without reproduction does not necessarily change the next generation’s gene pool.
terms.misconception: Every visit by an individual is automatically inherited gene flow.

terms.meaning: The introduction of new sequence variants through mutation.
terms.example: A heritable DNA change creates an allele not previously present at that locus.
terms.importantDistinction: Mutation is a source of new alleles; selection acts on their consequences.
terms.misconception: All mutations arise because they are needed.

terms.meaning: The degree to which populations exchange genetic contributions.
terms.example: Reproductive movement connects two habitat patches.
terms.importantDistinction: Physical connection is not the same as demonstrated successful gene flow.
terms.misconception: A visible corridor proves every population exchanges alleles equally.

terms.meaning: Differences in genetic composition among populations.

sections: Track successful contributions, not movement alone

Gene flow transfers alleles between populations. It can occur when individuals migrate and reproduce, or when gametes such as pollen move between populations. The important event is a genetic contribution to the recipient population.

An animal passing through a habitat without reproducing does not necessarily alter the next generation’s allele pool. Movement can create an opportunity, but successful reproduction connects that movement with inherited change.
Combine copies with the correct weights

Suppose 80 resident diploid breeders have A frequency 0.25 and 20 immigrant breeders have A frequency 0.75. If all contribute equally, residents supply 160 copies including 40 A; immigrants supply 40 copies including 30 A. The combined frequency is 70/200 = 0.35.

Do not take a simple average of 0.25 and 0.75 when the groups differ in size. Weight each frequency by the number of allele copies contributed. The equal-contribution assumption also matters: different reproductive success would change the weights.
Gene flow can add variation within a population and reduce genetic differences between populations, although the actual effect depends on their starting allele pools and contributions.
Mutation supplies new variants

Mutation changes DNA sequence and can create new alleles. A heritable mutation must enter the reproductive lineage to affect later generations. Many mutations have little effect in a particular setting; others can be harmful or beneficial.

Mutation and selection play different roles. Mutation generates sequence differences without knowing future need. Selection can favour or remove variants according to their reproductive consequences. Drift can also alter their frequencies, especially when a new variant is rare.

Isolation and habitat fragmentation can reduce opportunities for gene flow. A conservation argument about connectivity should therefore look for movement, successful reproduction and genetic evidence rather than assuming that a structure’s presence proves its effect.

lessons.title: Genetic diversity and conservation evidence
lessons.question: Why should population size and genetic variation be measured separately?
lessons.goal: Use population-genetic mechanisms to evaluate conservation evidence without assuming a universal outcome.
lessons.prior: Drift, selection, mutation and gene flow can act together. No single measurement describes every aspect of a population.

terms.meaning: The variety of genetic variants represented in a population or set of populations.
terms.example: A population contains several alleles at the loci examined.
terms.importantDistinction: A larger head count does not guarantee recovery of previously lost variants.
terms.misconception: Population size alone precisely measures all genetic diversity.

terms.meaning: Mating between genetically related individuals.
terms.example: Relatives are more likely to share copies inherited from a common ancestor.
terms.importantDistinction: It can increase homozygosity without creating harmful alleles on demand.
terms.misconception: Inbreeding creates every harmful allele from nothing.

terms.meaning: Observations used to evaluate a population’s condition and response to an action.
terms.example: Breeding success, survival, connectivity and genetic markers are measured together.
terms.importantDistinction: Several measures are needed to distinguish mechanisms and outcomes.
terms.misconception: A single attractive photograph proves a population is genetically secure.

terms.meaning: The capacity for heritable variation to support responses to changing conditions.
terms.example: Standing variation can provide different responses to a new challenge.
terms.importantDistinction: Genetic diversity can matter without guaranteeing survival under every change.
terms.misconception: A genetically diverse population cannot become extinct.

sections: A head count is only one measurement

A population can recover numerically after a bottleneck while retaining reduced genetic variation. Descendants multiply surviving allele copies; they do not automatically restore every lost variant. Population size and genetic diversity therefore answer different questions.

Small isolated populations may experience strong drift and increased mating among relatives. Inbreeding can increase homozygosity and expose effects of recessive alleles already present. It does not mean related individuals deliberately create new harmful alleles.
Connect a proposed action with its mechanism

A connection between habitats may permit movement and gene flow. If migrants reproduce, new alleles can enter a population and genetic differentiation may decline. Whether this happens depends on actual movement, survival and reproduction.

A population-management proposal should specify its biological mechanism and the evidence needed to evaluate it. Adding individuals, improving habitat and connecting populations are different interventions with potentially different effects.

The effects can include trade-offs. For example, introduced individuals may carry genetic variants suited to a different environment. An evidence-based evaluation considers both genetic contribution and the ecological setting rather than assuming that every transfer is beneficial.
Use cautious conclusions from limited data

Suppose a hypothetical monitoring report records more animals using a crossing structure and a rise in population size. That supports use of the structure and a demographic change. It does not alone establish increased gene flow or restored diversity at every locus.

Useful additional evidence might include successful breeding between populations, marker diversity, survival and the persistence of changes over generations. Sampling should be comparable across time.
Genetic diversity can support adaptive potential, but it is not a guarantee against extinction. Habitat, environmental change, population size and many other factors also matter.

A hypothetical crop line carries an introduced allele. Nearby compatible plants can potentially receive pollen, but no offspring genotypes have yet been measured.

Separate movement, inheritance and consequences
A marker can track allele presence while reproductive data evaluate contribution. Frequency change over generations can be measured separately from the allele’s ecological effects.

review.question: Can you distinguish a counted frequency, a model prediction and a causal explanation?

sections: Use the right method for the information

Genotype counts permit direct allele counting over 2N. Recessive phenotype information alone leaves some genotypes unknown, so a Hardy–Weinberg inference needs explicit assumptions. Expected genotype frequencies are p², 2pq and q² only within the model.
Keep frequencies distinct from counts. Multiply by population size only when an expected number is requested, and check that the complete categories total 1 or N as appropriate.
Interpret change without choosing a cause too soon

Selection links heritable variation with reproductive contribution; drift reflects chance; gene flow moves existing alleles between populations; mutation creates sequence variants. Non-random pairing can change genotype proportions without necessarily changing allele totals by itself.

A good population explanation uses the given evidence to distinguish these mechanisms. A small sample, an unexplained phenotype change or numerical recovery alone supports less than a complete claim about evolution or genetic diversity.
